title: IServiceScopeFactory (scoped work from singletons)
hook: Singletons like BackgroundService and IHostedService cannot inject scoped services directly. IServiceScopeFactory creates a short-lived scope so DbContext and other scoped services work safely outside HTTP requests.

blocks.text: IServiceScopeFactory is a singleton service registered by the framework that creates IServiceScope instances. Each scope has its own IServiceProvider where scoped services are resolved fresh and disposed when the scope ends. Background services, channel consumers, timer callbacks, and queue processors inject IServiceScopeFactory (not AppDbContext directly) and call CreateScope() for each unit of work — a message, a timer tick, or a batch job.

entries.plainDefinition: Singleton factory that creates disposable scopes for resolving scoped services outside request context.
A disposable scope with its own ServiceProvider. Dispose releases all scoped services.
A long-running IHostedService base class for background work in ASP.NET Core.
.NET extension that returns IAsyncDisposable scope for async disposal patterns.

blocks.text: Every production Web API eventually needs background work: processing an outbox table, consuming a message queue, running scheduled cleanup, or sending batched emails. All of these need DbContext — which is scoped. Injecting DbContext into BackgroundService is the captive dependency trap. IServiceScopeFactory is the canonical fix and a top FAANG interview question paired with the outbox pattern.

blocks.title: One scope per unit of work
blocks.body: Create a new scope for each message, timer tick, or batch — not one scope for the entire BackgroundService lifetime. A long-lived scope holds DbContext open indefinitely.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Scoped work in a background service

items.title: BackgroundService starts
items.body: Singleton worker injects IServiceScopeFactory (safe — factory itself is singleton).

items.title: Work item arrives
items.body: Message from queue or timer fires.

items.title: Create scope
items.body: using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope() — new scope per work item.

items.title: Resolve and work
items.body: Get AppDbContext and services from scope.ServiceProvider, do work, dispose scope.

diagram.title: IServiceScopeFactory in background processing
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant BG as BackgroundService\nsingleton
  participant SF as IServiceScopeFactory\nsingleton
  participant SC as IServiceScope
  participant DB as AppDbContext\nscoped
  BG->>SF: CreateScope()
  SF->>SC: new scope
  SC->>DB: resolve scoped
  BG->>DB: process message
  BG->>SC: Dispose()
  SC->>DB: dispose context

snippet.label: BackgroundService with per-message scope
snippet.explanation: IServiceScopeFactory is singleton-safe. Each message gets a fresh scope with its own DbContext. await using ensures async disposal.

snippet.label: Outbox pattern with scoped processing
snippet.explanation: Outbox dispatcher polls scoped DbContext per batch. Same request's data and outbox message share a transaction in the originating request scope; the dispatcher creates its own scope per poll cycle.

snippet.label: Timer callback and fire-and-forget scope
snippet.explanation: Each timer tick creates and disposes its own scope. Exception in one tick does not leak DbContext to the next tick.

snippet.label: Failure mode — long-lived scope in background service
snippet.explanation: Creating one scope in the constructor or field is as bad as injecting DbContext directly. The diagnostics counter active-db-contexts stuck at 1 confirms the bug.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: One scope for the entire BackgroundService lifetime. Forgetting to dispose the scope (use using/await using). Creating scope but resolving from root IServiceProvider. Running parallel work items sharing one scope without synchronization. Fire-and-forget Task.Run without its own scope.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore active-db-contexts during background processing — should spike per batch then return to baseline. OpenTelemetry traces showing DbContext span duration matching scope lifetime, not BackgroundService lifetime. Health check: background worker processes N messages, counter stays bounded. Integration test with WebApplicationFactory: enqueue message, assert DB updated, assert no ObjectDisposedException after 100 iterations. Pair with outbox pattern for reliable event publishing — same interview arc.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Third-party schedulers handle scope for you

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Injecting DbContext into BackgroundService without mentioning IServiceScopeFactory. One scope for the entire worker lifetime. Not knowing CreateAsyncScope exists. Unable to connect this to the outbox pattern or explain why queue consumers need per-message scopes.

interviewTakeaways: IServiceScopeFactory is singleton-safe — inject it into BackgroundService, not DbContext.
CreateScope() per work item (message, timer tick, batch) — never one scope for the service lifetime.
Production tip: monitor active-db-contexts during background processing; pair with outbox pattern for reliable events.

60s: BackgroundService is singleton. DbContext is scoped. Inject IServiceScopeFactory, call CreateScope per work item, resolve DbContext inside scope, dispose. Same fix for queue consumers and timer callbacks.
Follow-up: how do you handle parallel message processing — one scope per message or shared scope with locking?
commonPitfalls: DbContext in BackgroundService ctor gets you rejected — textbook captive dependency; IServiceScopeFactory is the expected answer.
One scope in ctor/field for entire worker — same bug, different shape.

Strong answer: 'Singleton worker, scoped work via IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope per unit of work. await using for async disposal. Outbox dispatcher polls with per-batch scope. NestJS uses ModuleRef.resolve for same pattern.'

jsTsCorrelations.concept: NestJS ModuleRef.resolve for request scope in cron
jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS cron jobs inject ModuleRef and call resolve(REQUEST-scoped provider) per execution — identical to IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope(). Without this, cron captures a single Prisma client forever.

jsTsCorrelations.concept: pg pool.connect per job in Node worker
jsTsCorrelations.note: Node background workers call pool.connect() per message and client.release() in finally — manual scope equivalent. Forgetting release() mirrors never disposing IServiceScope.
